q-37778.name: Question 1
q-37778.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
q-37778.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4,$ $q=-1$ and

$$
p+q=4+(-1)=3.
$$

q-37779.name: Question 2
q-37779.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
q-37779.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+9I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+9I) & =O \\ A-8I+9{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{8}{9}I-\frac{1}{9}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{8}{9},$ $q=-\frac{1}{9},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{8}{9}+(-\frac{1}{9})=\frac{7}{9}.
$$

First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{4}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}+3x-2,$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{2}$ $-$ $3x$ $+$ $11$
${x}^{2}+3x-2\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{4}\phantom{|}\,\,\,}$
${x}^{4}$ $+$ $3{x}^{3}$ $-$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ $3{x}^{3}$ $+$ $2{x}^{2}$
$-$ $3{x}^{3}$ $-$ $9{x}^{2}$ $+$ $6x$
$11{x}^{2}$ $-$ $6x$
$11{x}^{2}$ $+$ $33x$ $-$ $22$
$-$ $39x$ $+$ $22$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{4}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{4} & =q(x)p(x)+(-39x+22),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{2}-3x+11.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{4}=q(A)p(A)+(-39A+22I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & =q(A)p(A)+(-39A+22I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(-39A+22I) \\ & =-39A+22I.\end{aligned} $$

Question 5
?

If A is a 2×2 matrix A with characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2+3x−2, then A4=

a
−12A+53I
b
−21A+2I
c
−10A+7I
d
−39A+22I
e
30A+15I
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's divide the polynomial f(x)=x4 by characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2+3x−2, using long division:

x2 − 3x + 11
x2+3x−2 x4|
x4 + 3x3 − 2x2
− 3x3 + 2x2
− 3x3 − 9x2 + 6x
11x2 − 6x
11x2 + 33x − 22
− 39x + 22

Therefore, we can write x4 as

x4=q(x)p(x)+(−39x+22), where q(x)=x2−3x+11. Replacing x with A, we have

A4=q(A)p(A)+(−39A+22I).

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

A4=q(A)p(A)+(−39A+22I)=q(A)⋅O+(−39A+22I)=−39A+22I.
